name: Flavius Josephus
note:
**THE TRAITOR WHO PRESERVED US** — the roster's own epithet, and the whole difficulty.

Josephus commanded Jewish forces in Galilee, was besieged at Jotapata, survived a suicide pact in a cave by a lot he may have arranged, surrendered to Vespasian, took his patron's family name, and watched the Temple burn from the Roman side of the wall. Then he wrote the only surviving narrative account of all of it, in Rome, under Flavian protection.

**He is simultaneously the indispensable source for first-century Judaea and a man with pressing reasons to shape how that period was remembered.** Both halves are true and the room does not resolve them.

THE COMPLETE SURVIVING CORPUS IS HERE — four works, about 990,000 words: the *Antiquities* in twenty books, the *Wars* in seven, *Against Apion*, and the *Life*. There is no good reason to think he published anything else.

**THE TRANSLATION IS OLD AND NOT GOOD, AND IT IS HERE ANYWAY.** William Whiston's 1736 version is the only complete public-domain English Josephus, which is why every English reader has met this one. Whiston had no sound Greek text, his rendering is frequently at fault, and he cared little for style. **Treat it as a serviceable reading copy, not an authority on wording.**

**TWO DISPUTED PASSAGES ARE FLAGGED INSIDE THE TEXT.** Editorial warning blocks sit at Ant. XVIII.3.3 — the *Testimonium Flavianum* — and Ant. XX.9.1. They are searchable on the string 'DISPUTED PASSAGE' and are **not part of Whiston's text.** A room that reproduced the most argued-over paragraph in ancient literature without saying so would be doing the reader a disservice.

The *Antiquities* and the *Wars* are split by book — thirty-one files rather than two — because the single files ran to 2.9 MB and 1.3 MB and would not render in a browser. Nimrod's shelf on this site borrows Ant. I.4 for the tower of Babel.

works.title: The Life of Flavius Josephus
works.source: Flavius Josephus, *The Life of Flavius Josephus* · trans. William Whiston, 1736 · Project Gutenberg #2846 · public domain
works.note: The short autobiography appended to the *Antiquities* in the manuscripts, and the fourth of the four surviving works — **it was missing from this shelf and is now here.** He opens by establishing his priestly descent and spends much of it defending his conduct in Galilee against Justus of Tiberias. Read it as a defence brief, because that is what it is.

works.note: Creation to the death of Isaac. Josephus retelling Genesis for a Roman audience — and the retelling is the point: he is explaining a people to the empire that has just destroyed their temple.

works.source: Flavius Josephus, *Against Apion* · trans. William Whiston, 1736 · Project Gutenberg #2849 · public domain
works.note: Two books answering Greek writers who claimed the Jews had no antiquity worth the name. The most argumentative thing he wrote and the least self-exculpating — here he is defending a people rather than himself.
